This is definitely the likely near future of working in space, though an independent service robot this small might face some logistics challenges. Unless it employed some alternative propulsion, like electrodynamic tether systems, or had some orbital base to return to and refuel at, it might only be able to carry enough fuel to support a few service operations before becoming another piece of space junk itself.

NASA explored concepts largely identical to this going back into the early 1970s and for a time it was planned that the Space Station would be largely constructed by such telerobots using modular space frame construction. The origins of the NASA Robonaut can be found in this early plan. However, there was something of a rivalry between space centers in different states over the design of the station and management of its project and, with the finalization of the Shuttle design, an edict came down that the station would make no physical accommodations to robot use and that no robots would be used in or around it unless they could conform completely to human ergonomics and use exactly the same tools as human beings. That was largely impossible for the robotics technology of the time and so NASA's space telerobotics research was put on the slow track for decades. In the 90s a project called Ranger, building on developments with underwater ROVs, managed to produce some interesting prototypes put through their paces in NASA's neutral buoyancy facilities. Plans were made to test deploy the robots aboard the Space Shuttle in 1997, but this never happened and work was again put on the slow track. When NASA finally decided it 'needed' a telerobot at the ISS, they ended up buying it from Canada.

NASA seems to always develop this tech right to the edge of utility, then abandon it, probably because of their persistent belief that the public will not support them without astronaut/heroes to identify with. But it's always been clear to many that humans are never doing the heavy lifting in space and that telerobots are vital to our future out there. If we'd followed-through on the development, we'd be doing a hell of alot more out there at far less cost.
